q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated in ethanol, and the substitution product forms by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Which rate law describes this reaction?
h: Only species that appear in or before the rate-determining step show up in the rate law. What is the slow step of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction?
w: In an SN1 reaction the slow step is ionization of the C–Br bond to give the tertiary carbocation and Br−. Ethanol attacks the cation only afterward, in a fast step, so it does not appear in the rate law: rate = k[RBr]. (Ethanol is also the solvent, so its concentration barely changes anyway.)
x: A second-order rate law with the nucleophile is the S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law. Here ethanol adds after the rate-determining step, so its concentration does not enter.
The substrate must appear: its ionization is the rate-determining step. The nucleophile alone cannot control the rate.
No step involves two substrate molecules colliding; ionization is unimolecular, so the order in RBr is one.

q: The reaction of 1-bromopropane with NaCN in DMSO is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. If [NaCN] is tripled and [1-bromopropane] is halved, what happens to the initial rate?
c: It increases by a factor of 1.5
It increases by a factor of 3
It decreases to half of the original rate
It increases by a factor of 6
h: Write the rate law for an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction, then multiply the factor for each concentration change.
w: SN2 is a single concerted step involving both partners, so rate = k[RBr][CN−]. New rate = (½)(3) = 1.5 × the original rate.
x: Tripling the rate would be correct only if the substrate concentration did not appear in the rate law; in S<sub>N</sub>2 it does, and it was halved.
Halving the rate ignores the cyanide term; an S<sub>N</sub>2 rate is first order in the nucleophile too.
A factor of 6 comes from multiplying 3 × 2, treating "halved" as "doubled". Halving [RBr] contributes a factor of ½.

q: Initial rates were measured for the reaction of an alkyl bromide (RBr) with sodium azide in 80% aqueous ethanol. Which conclusion fits the data?
c: Rate = k[RBr]; an SN1 mechanism, as expected for a tertiary RBr
Rate = k[RBr][N3−]; an SN2 mechanism, as expected for a primary RBr
Rate = k[N3−]; an SN2 mechanism in which azide attack is slow
Rate = k[RBr]2; an SN1 mechanism with two ionizations
h: Compare experiments that change only one concentration at a time: 1 vs 2 for RBr, 1 vs 3 for azide.
w: Experiments 1 → 2: doubling [RBr] doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in RBr. Experiments 1 → 3: doubling [N3−] leaves the rate unchanged, so it is zero order in azide. Rate = k[RBr], the signature of an SN1 mechanism (rate-determining ionization). That fits a tertiary (or other cation-stabilizing) substrate in a polar protic solvent.
x: An S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law would double when [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] doubles; experiment 3 shows no change.
Experiment 2 shows the rate depends on [RBr], and experiment 3 shows it does not depend on azide; this choice has both backwards.
Doubling [RBr] would quadruple a second-order rate; the data show only a doubling.

q: Rank these alkyl bromides from slowest to fastest in an SN2 reaction with NaI in acetone.
h: S<sub>N</sub>2 needs backside access to the carbon bearing Br. Look at branching on that carbon (α) and on the next carbon (β).
w: SN2 rates fall as the backside of the electrophilic carbon gets crowded. Methyl (I) is fastest, then the unbranched primary 1-bromopropane (II), then the secondary 2-bromopropane (III). Neopentyl bromide (IV) is primary, but the tert-butyl group on the β carbon blocks the backside so completely that it reacts about 105 times slower than a simple primary halide, slower even than a secondary one. Order: IV < III < II < I.
x: This treats neopentyl bromide as a "normal" primary halide. Its β-tert-butyl group makes it slower than the secondary bromide III.
This is the S<sub>N</sub>1 (carbocation-stability) order turned around; for S<sub>N</sub>2 the least hindered methyl halide is fastest, not slowest.
Secondary III has an extra α-methyl group, so it is slower than the unbranched primary II, not faster.

q: Which compound undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis fastest in 80% aqueous ethanol?
h: The rate-determining step makes a carbocation. Which cation is stabilized by both alkyl groups and resonance?
w: SN1 rates follow carbocation stability. 2-Bromo-2-phenylpropane ionizes to a cation that is both tertiary and benzylic: the positive charge is delocalized into the ring and also stabilized by two methyl groups. 2-Bromo-2-phenylpropane is fastest.
x: The tert-butyl cation is tertiary but has no resonance; adding benzylic delocalization (the key) makes the cation more stable still.
The benzyl cation is resonance stabilized but primary; the tertiary benzylic cation has extra alkyl stabilization.
A secondary cyclohexyl cation has neither resonance nor tertiary substitution; it ionizes far more slowly.

q: Rank the halide ions from most to least nucleophilic toward CH3Br in methanol.
h: Methanol is a protic solvent. Which anion does it hydrogen-bond to most strongly?
w: In a polar protic solvent, small anions with concentrated charge are tightly hydrogen-bonded and must shed part of that solvent shell to react. F− is held most tightly and I− least; iodide is also the most polarizable. Nucleophilicity therefore runs I− > Br− > Cl− > F−, opposite to basicity.
x: This is the basicity order, and roughly the order in a polar aprotic solvent where anions are not hydrogen-bonded. Methanol is protic.
Iodide is not weaker than chloride in methanol; it is the least solvated and most polarizable halide, so it is the strongest of the four.
Bromide and iodide are reversed. Iodide, larger and more polarizable, is the better nucleophile in a protic solvent.

q: KCN reacts with 1-chlorobutane much faster in DMSO than in methanol. Which explanation is correct?
c: DMSO solvates K<sup>+</sup> well but cannot hydrogen-bond to CN<sup>−</sup>, leaving the anion poorly solvated and more reactive
DMSO hydrogen-bonds to CN<sup>−</sup>, which pulls electron density onto carbon and makes it more nucleophilic
DMSO stabilizes the butyl carbocation, so ionization of the C–Cl bond is faster
DMSO protonates the chlorine, turning it into a better leaving group
h: Think about what each solvent can do to an anion. Does DMSO have an O–H or N–H bond?
w: DMSO is polar aprotic: its partly negative oxygen solvates cations strongly, but it has no O–H to hydrogen-bond to anions. In methanol, CN− sits in a hydrogen-bonded cage that must be partly removed before it can attack. In DMSO the "naked" cyanide is higher in energy, so the SN2 barrier is lower. DMSO solvates K+ but not CN−.
x: DMSO has no O–H or N–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to anions; and hydrogen-bonding would lower, not raise, nucleophilicity.
A primary butyl cation is far too unstable to form; 1-chlorobutane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2, which has no carbocation.
DMSO is not an acid; it cannot protonate an alkyl chloride.

q: Rank the anions from best to worst leaving group.
h: A good leaving group is a weak base. Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> values of the conjugate acids.
w: Leaving-group ability tracks the stability of the departing anion, i.e., how weak a base it is. Conjugate-acid pKas: CF3SO3H ≈ −14, CH3SO3H ≈ −2, CH3CO2H 4.8, H2O 15.7. Triflate (II) has the charge spread over three oxygens and pulled further by the CF3 group. Order: II > III > I > IV.
x: The CF<sub>3</sub> group withdraws electron density inductively and makes triflate a weaker base than mesylate, so triflate leaves better.
Acetate is a much stronger base than either sulfonate (its acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8); it is a poor leaving group compared with them.
Hydroxide (from water, pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) is a far stronger base than acetate, so it is the worst leaving group, not third.

q: Which set of conditions converts 2-bromobutane mainly into a substitution product by an SN2 pathway?
h: A secondary substrate goes S<sub>N</sub>2 only with a good nucleophile that is a weak base, in a polar aprotic solvent.
w: With a secondary halide, strong bases (alkoxides) favor E2 elimination. Azide is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base (HN3 pKa 4.7), and DMSO leaves it unsolvated, so NaN3 in DMSO gives mainly 2-azidobutane by SN2 with inversion.
x: Ethoxide is a strong base; with a secondary bromide and heat, E2 (butenes) is the major pathway.
tert-Butoxide is a bulky strong base; it gives almost entirely E2 product with a secondary bromide.
Methanol is a weak nucleophile; with heat, a secondary bromide reacts slowly by S<sub>N</sub>1/E1, not S<sub>N</sub>2.

q:
Which changes would increase the rate of SN1 solvolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in ethanol?
I. Using 50% aqueous ethanol as the solvent
II. Adding 0.1 M NaN3, a much stronger nucleophile than ethanol
III. Replacing the chloride with bromide (2-bromo-2-methylpropane)
h: Ask what each change does to the energy of the ionization transition state.
w: The SN1 rate depends only on ionization. I: water is more polar and a better hydrogen-bond donor than ethanol; it stabilizes the developing carbocation and chloride, so ionization is faster. III: Br− is a weaker base and better leaving group than Cl−, so the C–Br bond ionizes faster. II: the nucleophile is not in the rate law, so adding azide changes which product forms (some tert-butyl azide) but not how fast the chloride ionizes. I and III only.
x: II does not raise the rate: any nucleophile, azide included, reacts only after the rate-determining ionization.
Adding a stronger nucleophile is the S<sub>N</sub>2 lever; S<sub>N</sub>1 is zero order in the nucleophile, and I and III do speed ionization.
A better leaving group also speeds the rate-determining ionization, so III belongs with I.

q: The energy diagram is for the S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction of a tertiary alkyl bromide with water. Which point is the carbocation intermediate?
c: B, the local minimum between two maxima
A, the highest point on the curve
The reactant energy level at the far left
h: Intermediates sit in energy wells; transition states sit at peaks.
w: An SN1 diagram has two steps: ionization (TS A, highest, rate-determining) and capture of the cation by water (TS C, low). The carbocation sits in the valley between them, at B. It is a real species with a finite lifetime, unlike a transition state.
x: A is the transition state for ionization, the rate-determining step. A transition state is a maximum, not an intermediate.
C is the transition state for nucleophile capture of the cation; it is a maximum.
The far-left level is the starting alkyl bromide plus water, before any bond breaks.

q: Which description of the S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state for CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is correct?
c: The carbon is roughly trigonal bipyramidal, with O and Br partly bonded on opposite sides
The central carbon is a planar carbocation, with Br<sup>−</sup> fully detached and CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup> not yet bonded
O and Br are partly bonded on the same side of the central carbon, about 90° apart
The central carbon is tetrahedral, with five full bonds to its five groups
h: S<sub>N</sub>2 is concerted and goes with inversion. Where must the nucleophile be relative to the leaving group?
w: In the SN2 transition state the nucleophile enters from the back while the leaving group departs from the front: O···C···Br is nearly linear (180°), and the three other groups lie flat in a plane, like an umbrella turning inside out. Trigonal bipyramidal, O and Br partly bonded on opposite sides. This geometry is why SN2 inverts configuration.
x: A free carbocation is the S<sub>N</sub>1 intermediate. S<sub>N</sub>2 has no intermediate; bond making and breaking happen together.
Frontside attack would give retention; S<sub>N</sub>2 uses backside attack, with the nucleophile 180° from the leaving group.
Carbon cannot have five full bonds; in the transition state the C–O and C–Br bonds are both partial.

q: Which list contains only polar aprotic solvents?
h: Protic solvents have an H on O or N. Polar solvents have a sizable dipole.
w: Dimethyl sulfoxide, N,N-dimethylformamide, acetone and acetonitrile all have strong dipoles (S=O, C=O, C≡N) but no O–H or N–H bonds. DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile is the all-aprotic polar list.
x: Methanol has an O–H bond; it is polar protic.
Water, acetic acid and ethanol are all polar protic; only DMF is aprotic.
Hexane and toluene are nonpolar, and diethyl ether is only weakly polar; DMSO is the only polar aprotic solvent in the list.

q: 3-Bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane is heated in ethanol. Which compound is the major substitution product?
h: A secondary carbocation next to a quaternary carbon can become more stable by a 1,2-shift. Which group can move?
w: Ionization gives a secondary cation at C3. The adjacent C2 carries three methyl groups (no H), so a 1,2-methyl shift moves the cation to C2, where it is tertiary. Ethanol captures this tertiary cation: 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane. (E1 alkenes also form, but the question asks for the substitution product.)
x: This is the unrearranged ether. The secondary cation rearranges to a tertiary one faster than ethanol captures it.
This is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, an E1 elimination product, not a substitution product.
D would need the cation on a primary carbon; shifts go toward the more stable cation, not away from it.

q: 3-Chloro-3-methylbut-1-ene is dissolved in aqueous acetone. Which statement best describes the alcohol products of S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis?
c: Both 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol and 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol, from water attacking either end of the allylic cation
Only 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol forms, because water attacks only the tertiary carbon that lost Cl<sup>−</sup>
Only 3-methylbutan-2-ol forms, after a hydride shift
Only 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol forms, by direct S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of water at the less hindered primary carbon atom
h: Draw the cation formed by ionization. Is the positive charge on one carbon only?
w: Loss of Cl− gives a cation that is both tertiary and allylic. Resonance spreads the positive charge over C3 (tertiary) and C1 (primary end of the old alkene). Water can attack either site, giving 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol and 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol. The second product has a trisubstituted (more stable) C=C, so it is an important product even though attack occurs at a primary carbon.
x: The allylic cation is delocalized, so water can also attack C1; ignoring the second resonance form misses a major product.
That product is saturated: a hydride shift cannot remove a C=C, and the allylic tertiary cation has no reason to rearrange.
The starting material has no leaving group on a primary carbon; C1 is sp<sup>2</sup>. The primary alcohol comes from the resonance-delocalized cation, not from S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Rank the nucleophiles from most to least reactive toward CH3I in methanol.
h: Two rules: an anion beats its neutral conjugate acid, and in a protic solvent a larger, more polarizable atom beats a smaller one in the same group.
w: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen and is less tightly hydrogen-bonded by methanol, so CH3S− is the best. Among the oxygen nucleophiles, methoxide (localized charge, strong base) beats acetate (charge delocalized over two oxygens), and neutral methanol is weakest. Order: CH3S− > CH3O− > CH3CO2− > CH3OH.
x: This follows basicity. In a protic solvent, the more polarizable, less solvated thiolate is the better nucleophile even though methoxide is the stronger base.
Acetate is resonance stabilized, which makes it a weaker nucleophile than methoxide, not a stronger one.
Thiolate is the strongest of the four in methanol; placing it below acetate ignores polarizability.

q: Which compound reacts readily both by S<sub>N</sub>1 (ethanol, heat) and by S<sub>N</sub>2 (NaI in acetone)?
h: S<sub>N</sub>1 needs a stabilized cation; S<sub>N</sub>2 needs an unhindered carbon. Which substrate offers both?
w: Benzyl bromide is primary, so the backside is open for SN2; it is also benzylic, so the SN2 transition state and the SN1 cation are both stabilized by the ring π system. Benzyl bromide reacts quickly by either path.
x: tert-Butyl bromide ionizes easily (S<sub>N</sub>1) but its crowded tertiary carbon blocks backside attack, so it does not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2.
1-Bromobutane is a fine S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate, but a primary unstabilized cation is too high in energy for S<sub>N</sub>1.
Bromobenzene reacts by neither: backside attack would go through the ring, and an aryl cation is very unstable.
